Cautiously positive overall, with support from monetary policy transmission and anchored inflation expectations, but tempered by weak capex and external headwinds. The 25 bp rate cut and liquidity operations (T-bill purchases and repos to maintain ample reserves) align with evidence that policy affects real activity via the interest-rate and liquidity channels (Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans 2005; McCallum and Nelson 1999; Sims 1992). Business fixed investment is typically interest-sensitive and depends on internal finance, so easing and smoother money markets should help, though financing frictions mean investment may respond only gradually (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994). With inflation below 2% and market-based inflation compensation low, the New Keynesian framework—where inflation depends on expected future inflation and the output gap—supports measured easing to close the gap without large inflation risk (Galí and Gertler 1999; Woodford 2003). The Desk’s actions mitigate money-market pressures, reinforcing implementation and the liquidity effect. Strong labor markets and resilient household spending keep the expansion intact, but global developments and weak capex keep risks tilted to the downside.
